name: Fawn
lede: Fawn is a light yellowish brown named for the coat of a young deer, and Renaissance color writers had a lot to say about it.

sections.title: A deer's coat
sections.body:
Paterson defines fawn as a light yellowish brown, the coat color of a young deer [1]. The swatch here is a pinkish tan, near [[camel]], [[tan]] and [[beige]], and lighter than [[auburn]].

In hunting, the animals the court hunted were fawn-colored deer, red foxes and young boars, or black bears and old boars, in Pastoureau's account of hunt dress [2].

sections.title: Renaissance color advice
sections.body:
One Renaissance writer on color combinations, as Pastoureau reports, counted grey with fawn, in Italian *leonato*, among the most beautiful pairs [3]. Pastoureau also reports that in the French color-ranking of Robertet, tanné, a fawn-colored or dark russet, came after purple, and an anonymous successor called it the ugliest of colors [4]. Robertet himself held it changeable and unreliable [4].

As a pigment name, Mayer describes fawn brown as a mixture of burnt or raw umber with dark ochre [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds fawn in 583 of 23,781 paintings, 2.45 percent, as photographed [6]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 39 of 1,674 paintings, about 1.6 times the baseline [6]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light [6]. The most devoted painter is Maurice Denis, in 5 of 43 works here [6]. It shares canvases with Cameo Brown and Desert Sand [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so this is a color match, not a pigment test [6].
